findings.statement: CXCR1 and CXCR2 are proposed as neutrophil extracellular trap-related treatment targets in UC on the basis of Mendelian randomization, colocalization and transcriptomic analysis (title-level evidence in a single study). A separate eQTL/pQTL/transcriptome study ties the CXCL5/CXCR2 axis to neutrophil chemotaxis and immune activation in UC. The top-ranked gene has no verbatim-validated relation in the graph, so the support is indirect and genetic or bioinformatic only, with no UC clinical trial evidence in this corpus.

One review-type sentence states that the CXCL8-CXCR1 and CXCR2 axis participates in UC pathogenesis through PI3K/Akt, MAPK and NF-kappaB signaling. In blood RNA-seq validation for IBD, CXCL8 was reported as one of the best diagnostic genes, second to ITGA5. CXCL8 was also a PPI hub gene in a UC bioinformatic study. Evidence is mechanistic or bioinformatic, not interventional.

A single preclinical study reports IDO1 elevated in UC patients and colitis mice, driving pro-inflammatory macrophage polarization via an ER stress pathway. An IDO1 inhibitor (methyl-tryptophan) ameliorated DSS colitis weight loss, colon shortening and severity. This is one mouse and human-data study, so the support is preclinical and the result is not replicated in this corpus.

MMP1 was reported with strong diagnostic potential in a study of UC-associated CRC (single bioinformatic study, the AUC was not tied to a field here), and ilomastat was only predicted in silico as an MMP1 inhibitor by docking. Mirikizumab-modified transcripts, including MMP1, MMP3, S100A8 and IL1B, correlate with Mayo, Geboes and Robarts disease activity indices, which supports MMP1 as a treatment-response and activity marker rather than a validated target.

CHI3L1 was upregulated in UC patients and correlated with NLRP3 inflammasome expression, and it promoted macrophage pyroptosis through the BCAT1/NF-kappaB axis. Inhibiting CHI3L1 was protective in that study. Velpatasvir binding to recombinant CHI3L1 was shown by microscale thermophoresis, which gives an early repurposing lead. The evidence is preclinical, from a small number of studies.

DUOX2 protein was among the most elevated in inflamed UC biopsies versus healthy controls in a proteomic study, alongside LCN2. DUOX2 was listed with S100A8, IL1B, CXCL1, MMP10 and others as a credible diagnostic and therapeutic biomarker in a bioinformatic study. A herbal formula (TLXDS) was reported to act by inhibiting DUOX2, so DUOX2 is a mechanism and biomarker candidate with no drug in the clinic.

S100A9 expression was reported to perform excellently in diagnosing active UC (ROC analysis, one study) and was overexpressed in colitis mice. In a tofacitinib single-cell study, response was associated with downregulation of S100A9, FCGR3A and MMP12 in resident macrophages. The signal is largely neutrophil and myeloid, so it reflects infiltrating inflammatory cells rather than epithelial change.

AQP9 was predominantly expressed in neutrophils and upregulated in UC colon of mice and in PMA-stimulated neutrophils. In that study, neutrophil AQP9 promoted NET formation through JAK2-STAT3-mediated pyroptosis and aggravated epithelial injury. The signal is neutrophil-derived, from a single preclinical study, and no drug targets AQP9.

TREM1 signaling was reported to amplify neutrophil-mediated inflammation in IBD. TREM1 activation exacerbates colitis in mice. In patient biopsies an elevated TREM1 pathway signature is associated with inflamed tissue and treatment resistance in UC. This is a recent single study. TREM1 has no verbatim-validated relation in the graph, only abstract chunks.

CD274, MMP1, NCF2 and PLAU were proposed as hub genes associated with UC, positively associated with macrophage infiltration in a bioinformatic analysis. CD274 has no verbatim-validated relation in the graph despite high Open Targets literature and genetic scores, so the supporting literature in this corpus is thin and signature-level only.

SLC26A3 was significantly lower in UC than in controls in ONT RNA-seq analysis. Epithelial transport and metabolic genes such as HMGCS2 (decreased in UC with high diagnostic value reported) and AQP8 (decreased) are downregulated, which reflects loss of epithelial and colonocyte function. This loss-of-function direction suggests restoration rather than inhibition, and the literature supports these only as diagnostic markers.

LCN2 was higher in UC than in controls and was reported as a potential diagnostic biomarker for UC-associated carcinogenesis related to disease duration. Within the study, LCN2 fell from short-duration UC to long-duration UC to UC-associated cancer, so it is not monotonic with neoplasia. LCN2 was also elevated in inflamed UC biopsies at protein level.

Tofacitinib, a JAK inhibitor, is described as approved for moderate-to-severe UC, which gives pathway-level clinical validation. Many herbal or acupuncture studies report suppression of the JAK2/STAT3 pathway in DSS colitis, but these are low-quality preclinical reports. JAK2 itself has no verbatim-validated relation in the graph.

caveats: Most genes rank high from expression and Open Targets signals; CXCR2, CXCR1, CD274, JAK2, TREM1, CXCL5, REG1A, PI3, CLDN2, FCGR2A and INHBA have no verbatim-validated literature relations in the graph (only chunk titles or none).
Most literature is bioinformatic hub-gene analysis or DSS mouse work; very few clinical-trial reports appear. No trial of CXCR1 or CXCR2 antagonists in UC was found in this corpus.
Neutrophil and myeloid genes (S100A8/9, AQP9, CXCL8, LCN2, TREM1) may reflect infiltrating cells, not tissue change.
Numeric values from sentences (AUCs) were not bound to record fields and are left out; the findings are descriptive.
No contradictory findings were observed in the retrieved sentences, but the corpus is small (about 300 abstracts) and silence is not evidence of absence.
